title: IDToolkit: A Toolkit for Benchmarking and Developing Inverse Design Algorithms in Nanophotonics

problem.claim: AI and machine learning methods could aid scientific design, but scientific design involves complex domain knowledge and professional skills for experiments and evaluations.

gap.claim: These domain and evaluation obstacles prevent AI researchers from developing specialized methods for scientific design.

contributions.claim: A computationally verifiable benchmark is proposed for inverse design of nanophotonic devices.
The benchmark implements three nanophotonic design problems with differing design parameter spaces, complexity, and design targets, using an open-source simulator.
Ten inverse design algorithms are implemented and compared in a reproducible and fair framework.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the results revealed strengths and weaknesses of existing methods and suggested future directions for more efficient inverse design algorithms.
The authors report that the benchmark can serve as a starting point for more challenging scientific design problems.
The authors report that the IDToolkit code is available in a public GitHub repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: AI and machine learning may assist scientific design, but domain knowledge and experimental skills create barriers.
The work proposes a computationally verifiable benchmark for inverse design in nanophotonics.
The benchmark covers three distinct nanophotonic design problems and uses an open-source simulator.
Ten inverse design algorithms are compared in a reproducible and fair framework.
The authors report method strengths and weaknesses, future research directions, and broader use as a starting point for challenging scientific design problems.

source_observation.claim: The benchmark varies design parameter spaces, complexity, and design targets across three nanophotonic problems.

interpretation.claim: Evaluation across structurally different problem settings can expose method-specific strengths and weaknesses.

application.claim: When developing scientific-design algorithms, construct benchmarks that include multiple problem characteristics rather than a single task.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this lesson generalizes beyond nanophotonic inverse design.

source_observation.claim: The algorithms are compared using an open-source simulator and a reproducible, fair framework.

interpretation.claim: Shared computational environments can reduce barriers to reproducible comparison when physical experiments are difficult.

application.claim: Use openly available simulation environments and standardized comparison procedures to support repeatable algorithm evaluation.

exception.claim: Computational verification may not capture all requirements of experimental scientific design.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the ten algorithms, datasets, metrics, or quantitative comparison results.
The abstract does not describe benchmark implementation details, computational verification procedures, or experimental validation.
